facts.text: A Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) is a single overarching document that ties every planned virtual or physical test to the decision it informs, required data, resources, schedule and pass criteria.
facts.quote: A Test and Evaluation Master Plan (TEMP) is the single overarching document that ties every planned test, virtual or physical, to the decision it informs, the data it needs, its resources, its schedule and its pass criteria.

facts.text: The United States Department of Defense requires a TEMP for major programs under DoD Instruction 5000.89 of November 2020 and the TEMP Guidebook version 3.1 of January 2017.
facts.quote: The United States Department of Defense requires a TEMP for its major programs (DoD Instruction 5000.89 of November 2020 and the TEMP Guidebook version 3.1 of January 2017).

facts.text: A TEMP links program decisions to test objectives, metrics, data needs, resources, schedule, entrance and exit criteria and reporting.
facts.quote: The document links program decisions to test objectives, metrics, data needs, resources, schedule, entrance and exit criteria and reporting.

facts.text: The core device of a TEMP is the Integrated Decision Support Key: for each decision, state the evaluation question and then the data required to answer it.
facts.quote: Its core device is the Integrated Decision Support Key: for each decision, state the evaluation question, then the data required to answer it.

facts.text: Defense test practice treats modeling-and-simulation verification and validation as part of the integrated test strategy rather than an isolated exercise, providing a precedent against separate simulation and physical-test teams.
facts.quote: The defense practice also treats modeling-and-simulation verification and validation as part of the integrated test strategy rather than an isolated exercise

facts.text: Outcome studies comparing TEMP use with alternatives were not found.

facts.text: A literal defense TEMP would be excessive for the eleven-month collision-mitigation validation program.
facts.quote: a literal defense TEMP would be excessive for an eleven-month program.

facts.text: The transferable TEMP practice for the collision-mitigation program is an integrated virtual and physical test strategy with one line per claim specifying the decision, required evidence, test or model method, comparator, acceptance rule, data, owner and date.
facts.quote: The transferable idea is an integrated virtual and physical test strategy with one line per claim: decision to be informed, evidence required, test or model method, comparator, acceptance rule, data, owner, date

facts.text: The collision-mitigation program should plan the four months after prototype arrival as a physical correlation window, first measuring latency, detection range, brake timing and stopping dynamics on the real machine and then updating the models.
facts.quote: planning the four months after the prototype arrives as a physical correlation window: first measure latency, detection range, brake timing and stopping dynamics on the real machine, update the models

facts.text: After real-machine measurements and model updates, the collision-mitigation program should use virtual regression to run the large scenario matrix while physical machines focus on boundary conditions and worst cases.

facts.text: Every documented virtualization of automatic braking retained physical referents.

facts.text: The collision-mitigation test plan must separately state what virtual evidence will explore, screen, verify, validate or replace; reducing physical testing and taking safety credit instead of physical testing are very different claims.
